key_facts: The chapter covers: Connectivity (Paths and Circuits), Euler and Hamilton Paths, the Shortest Path Problem (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Ford's algorithm), and Graph Coloring.
A cut vertex (articulation point) is a vertex whose removal disconnects the graph; in Vietnamese: 'đỉnh cắt' hay 'điểm khớp'.
An Euler path is a path that traverses every edge of the graph exactly once; a Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once.
Shortest path algorithms covered include Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford algorithm, and Floyd-Warshall algorithm.

The material is authored by Huynh Tuong Nguyen, Tran Tuan Anh, Nguyen An Khuong, and Le Hong Trang from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Technology - VNUHCM, dated August 16, 2021.
A Hamilton circuit is defined as a circuit that visits each vertex in a graph exactly once.

Three rules of Hamilton Circuits are taught: (Rule 1) if deg(v) = 2, both edges incident to v must be used; (Rule 2) no subcircuit can be formed; (Rule 3) once two edges at a vertex v are determined, all other edges incident at v must be removed.
Property of Dijkstra's Algorithm: applicable for any graph G with any edge length ℓ(vi) ≥ 0, one-to-all shortest paths, time complexity O(|V|²).
Dijkstra's algorithm CAN be used on directed graphs (digraphs), but CANNOT be used on graphs with negative edge weights.

An application of Hamilton circuits is generating Gray Code: an n-digit Gray code can be generated by finding Hamilton circuits of an n-dimensional hypercube; Gray code is used in digital communication to reduce the effect of noise.
generated_text: Understanding Graph Connectivity In the study of graphs, one of the most fundamental questions we can ask is whether the graph is "in one piece." This concept is known as connectivity. This lesson explores what it means for a graph to be connected, how we can measure the robustness of that connection, and how connectivity is defined for different types of graphs. Connectedness in Undirected Graphs The most basic form of connectivity applies to undirected graphs. Definition: An undirected graph is called connected if there is a path between every pair of distinct vertices of the graph. A key property is that if a graph is connected, there is always a simple path between every pair of distinct vertices. If a graph is not connected, it is called a disconnected graph . A disconnected graph is composed of two or more connected components , which are the separate, connected subgraphs. How Connected is a Graph? Beyond simply being connected or not, we can measure how "strongly" connected a graph is. This is done by identifying critical vertices and edges that, if removed, would break the graph apart. Key Terms: A cut vertex (or articulation point) is a vertex whose removal increases the number of connected components in the graph. A cut edge (or bridge) is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components. We can also quantify a graph's connectivity: A graph that has no cut vertices is called a nonseparable graph . The vertex connectivity of a graph G, denoted κ(G), is the minimum number of vertices in a vertex cut (a set of vertices whose removal disconnects the graph). The edge connectivity of a graph G, denoted λ(G), is the minimum number of edges in an edge cut (a set of edges whose removal disconnects the graph). For example, if the minimum number of vertices that must be removed to disconnect a graph is 2 (e.g., vertices {c, f}), then its vertex connectivity κ(G) = 2. If the minimum number of edges is 3 (e.g., edges {{b, c}, {a, f}, {f, g}}), then its edge connectivity λ(G) = 3. Connectedness in Directed Graphs For directed graphs, the concept of connectivity is more nuanced because the direction of edges matters. Definition: A directed graph is strongly connected if there is a path from any vertex to any other vertex in the graph, respecting the direction of the edges (i.e., a path from a to b and a path from b to a ). A directed graph is weakly connected if there is a path between any two vertices in the underlying undirected graph (i.e., if we ignore the direction of the edges). Summary In this lesson, we defined graph connectivity and its different forms: Connected Undirected Graph: A path exists between every pair of vertices. A graph can be connected or disconnected, with the latter consisting of connected components. Measuring Connectivity: We use cut vertices, cut edges, vertex connectivity (κ(G)), and edge connectivity (λ(G)) to understand a graph's resilience. Connected Directed Graph: We distinguish between strongly connected (paths exist in both directions between any two vertices) and weakly connected (the underlying undirected graph is connected).
